---
title: "Figure 14.1: LA8 excl. Mexico: Structural Primary Balance and Commodity Terms of Trade"
---

![Python: `python/fig-14-1.py`](../images/python/fig-14-1.png)

The average structural primary balance of seven Latin American countries
(LA8 excluding Mexico), with its min–max range across countries, on the left
scale. Commodity terms of trade (CTOT) are on the right scale. The chart
asks whether fiscal balances move with commodity prices: when export prices
are high, governments in commodity exporters tend to run larger surpluses.

**New in this chart:** a band and a right-hand scale together. Both
techniques were explained on earlier pages: the band in
[Figure 15.2](fig-15-2.qmd) and [Figure 1.2.2](fig-1-2-2.qmd), the
right-hand scale in [Figure 5.1](fig-5-1.qmd). This page shows how they
combine.

## The data

Sheet `data`, 23 rows (2005 to 2027):

| category | Min | Min-Max range | Structural primary balance | CTOT (index: 2000 = 100; right scale) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2005 | 0.15 | 6.04 | 3.46 | 101.0 |

- `Min` and `Min-Max range` are the two helper series of Excel's stacked
  area: the bottom of the band, and its width. See [Shaded
  bands](../techniques.qmd#sec-bands).
- `Structural primary balance` is the average, drawn as the purple line.
- The CTOT column has the longest name in the book. It is the Excel series
  name, which doubles as the legend label.

## The script

### Long column names

```python
data = read_chart_data(STEM)
years = data["category"]

balance = "Structural primary balance"
ctot = "CTOT (index: 2000 = 100; right scale)"
colours = {balance: "#5B2A78", ctot: "#A2A39D"}
```

The long column names are stored once, in `balance` and `ctot`, and the
colour dictionary uses them as keys. From here on the script writes
`data[ctot]` instead of the full name. That is shorter, and if the name
changes in a new edition, it only has to be changed in one place.

The balance is purple and CTOT grey. Grey is a common choice for the
right-scale series: it is the secondary, context series, and the colour
says so.

### The frame

`new_chart()` gets a two-line title and a nine-line caption, so the plot
area is fairly short. `right=0.4` leaves room for the right-hand labels
(100 to 105), and `bottom_gap=0.4` for the vertical year labels.

### The layers

```python
# In Excel the shaded range is a stacked area: "Min" plus "Min-Max range".
ax.fill_between(years, data["Min"], data["Min"] + data["Min-Max range"],
                color="#E9DFEE", linewidth=0)
ax.axhline(0, color="black", linewidth=0.7)
ax.plot(years, data[balance], color=colours[balance], linewidth=2.0)

ax_right = add_right_axis(ax, (100, 105), 1)
ax_right.plot(years, data[ctot], color=colours[ctot], linewidth=2.0)
ax_right.tick_params(axis="y", length=2.8)
```

The drawing is built up in layers, from back to front:

1. **The band**, in a pale purple, from `Min` to `Min` plus the range.
   `linewidth=0` removes its outline.
2. **A line at zero**, which separates surpluses from deficits. It is drawn
   after the band, so it stays visible where the band crosses zero.
3. **The balance line**, on the left scale, in the dark purple of the
   band's hue.
4. **CTOT**, on a right-hand scale from 100 to 105 with a tick every 1.
   `add_right_axis()` creates a second axes object, `ax_right`, on top of
   `ax`. Anything drawn on `ax_right` therefore lies on top of all the
   layers on `ax`. See [A right-hand
   scale](../chart-style.qmd#sec-right-axis).

The band, the zero line and the balance all belong to `ax`, so they share
the left scale. Only CTOT uses the right one.

### The axes

```python
ax.set_xlim(2004.5, 2027.5)
ax.set_xticks(range(2005, 2028, 2))
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelrotation=90, length=2.8)

set_y_scale(ax, -12, 8, 4)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=2.8)
```

- **The x-axis** runs half a year beyond the first and last points, with a
  label every second year (2005, 2007, ..., 2027), written vertically.
- **The left scale** runs from -12 to 8 in steps of 4: -12, -8, -4, 0, 4, 8.
  That is five intervals, matching the five steps of 1 on the right (100 to
  105), so each tick on the left is level with one on the right. Zero on the
  left lines up with 103 on the right.

Note that the x-limits are set on `ax` only. `ax_right` shares the x-axis,
so it follows automatically.

### The legend

```python
ax.legend([Line2D([], [], color=c, linewidth=2.0) for c in colours.values()],
          list(colours), loc="lower left", bbox_to_anchor=(0.03, 0.03),
          handlelength=3.0, labelspacing=0.2)
```

The two lines are on different axes objects, so the legend is built from
sample lines, one per colour in the `colours` dictionary, with the
dictionary's keys as the labels. See [A right-hand
scale](../techniques.qmd#sec-right-scale).

The band is not in the legend. The caption says what it is, as in the
published chart.

This legend is placed on `ax`, not on `ax_right` as in most two-scale
charts. That works because it sits in the lower left, just below where the
grey CTOT line on `ax_right` starts (101 on the right scale, about a fifth
of the way up). If the CTOT line ran through that corner,
it would be drawn over the legend; the fix would be to call
`ax_right.legend(...)` instead.

## Changing the chart

- **The band in the legend.** Add a filled patch as a third entry:

  ```python
  from matplotlib.patches import Patch
  handles = [Line2D([], [], color=c, linewidth=2.0) for c in colours.values()]
  handles.append(Patch(color="#E9DFEE"))
  ax.legend(handles, [*colours, "Min-max range"], ...)
  ```

- **A wider right scale.** If CTOT moves outside 100–105, keep five
  intervals, for example `add_right_axis(ax, (95, 110), 3)`.

## The complete script

The full `python/fig-14-1.py`, as it runs:

```` {.python filename="python/fig-14-1.py"}
"""Figure 14.1: LA8 excl. Mexico: Structural Primary Balance and Commodity Terms of Trade."""
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D

from chart_style import (
    add_right_axis,
    new_chart,
    read_chart_data,
    save_chart,
    set_y_scale,
)

STEM = "fig-14-1"

data = read_chart_data(STEM)
years = data["category"]

balance = "Structural primary balance"
ctot = "CTOT (index: 2000 = 100; right scale)"
colours = {balance: "#5B2A78", ctot: "#A2A39D"}

fig, ax = new_chart(
    title="LA8 excl. Mexico: Structural Primary Balance and\nCommodity Terms of Trade",
    subtitle="(Percent of GDP; unless noted otherwise)",
    caption=(
        "Sources: IMF, Commodity Terms of Trade database; IMF, World\n"
        "Economic Outlook database; and IMF staff calculations.\n"
        "Note: Structural primary balance is simple average. Chile refers to the\n"
        "central government’s structural non-mining primary balance. Colombia\n"
        "refers to the consolidated public sector’s structural non-oil primary\n"
        "balance. Peru refers to the nonfinancial public sector’s structural primary\n"
        "balance. CTOT is purchasing-power-parity GDP-weighted average. CTOT\n"
        "= commodity terms of trade; LA8 = Latin America 8 (Argentina, Brazil,\n"
        "Chile, Colombia, Mexico, Paraguay, Peru, Uruguay)."
    ),
    left=0.35,
    right=0.4,
    bottom_gap=0.4,
)

# In Excel the shaded range is a stacked area: "Min" plus "Min-Max range".
ax.fill_between(years, data["Min"], data["Min"] + data["Min-Max range"],
                color="#E9DFEE", linewidth=0)
ax.axhline(0, color="black", linewidth=0.7)
ax.plot(years, data[balance], color=colours[balance], linewidth=2.0)

ax_right = add_right_axis(ax, (100, 105), 1)
ax_right.plot(years, data[ctot], color=colours[ctot], linewidth=2.0)
ax_right.tick_params(axis="y", length=2.8)

ax.set_xlim(2004.5, 2027.5)
ax.set_xticks(range(2005, 2028, 2))
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelrotation=90, length=2.8)

set_y_scale(ax, -12, 8, 4)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=2.8)

ax.legend([Line2D([], [], color=c, linewidth=2.0) for c in colours.values()],
          list(colours), loc="lower left", bbox_to_anchor=(0.03, 0.03),
          handlelength=3.0, labelspacing=0.2)

save_chart(fig, STEM)
````
